name: Frugality
definition: Accomplish more with less. Constraints breed resourcefulness, self-sufficiency, and invention. There are no extra points for growing headcount, budget size, or fixed expense.
why: Frugality is not being cheap. It is spending on what matters to customers and to the long-term health of the business. The cheapest move is to turn the product off. That saves a lot of money, and it kills the company. Most spending decisions are less dramatic than that, and they still have the same shape: spend where it makes you faster, better, or more useful to the customer.

Look for resourcefulness, not deprivation. Buying junk hardware that slows every builder is not frugality. It is being cheap in a way that costs more later. Skipping the trip that keeps a builder from building is the same mistake. Constraints should force invention, not chew through the two-by-fours.

Many problems go away if you throw cash at them. That is why the constraint is useful. If traffic grows 135 percent and you refuse to grow the budget by the same amount, you have to reinvent how you scale, build, and deploy. The invention is the point. Headcount, budget, and fixed expense are not scoreboard categories.

Frugality also means you will take a five million dollar hit now for a $50 million payout later, and you will not spend the leftover budget in December so nobody cuts you next year. The budget is an input. It is not the decision.
calibrationIntro: Score whether someone invents under constraint and still invests in what matters. Under is waste and entitlement. Over is penny-pinching that starves builders, customers, or the long term.

rows.situation: When the obvious path is to buy the thing
rows.under: Spends too much and treats money as the first solution.
rows.justRight: Understands the cost, then looks for a way to get the outcome without the spend, or with much less of it.
rows.over: Refuses to spend on anything and starves the chance to invent.

rows.situation: When the team talks about resources
rows.under: No controls. A sense of entitlement. People spend as if the money is free.
rows.justRight: Builds a habit of asking how the work uses time, people, and money, and what return that spend should earn. That is {lp:ownership}.
rows.over: Skips needed investment. Refuses to pay people as a meritocracy in the name of saving money.

rows.situation: When someone on the team is hurt or stuck far from home
rows.under: Pays for first class on a routine trip and calls it taking care of people.
rows.justRight: Gets the person the care they need and the next available commercial flight home. Spends what the situation requires, not what looks generous.
rows.over: Forces the person to wait for a cheaper routing while they are hurt or unable to finish the work.

rows.under: Buys all the hardware the team might need and never re-engineers the service to be cheaper to run.
rows.justRight: Sets an aggressive infrastructure target that forces invention in how the service is built and run.
rows.over: Cuts hardware so hard that availability and the customer experience break.

rows.situation: When a spend looks good this quarter
rows.under: Big spends on things that do not last.
rows.justRight: Balances near-term benefit with long-term sustainability.
rows.over: Penny-pinches to hit this quarter's number and damages the next three years.

rows.situation: When the budget becomes the argument
rows.under: Spends the maximum so the budget is not cut next year.
rows.justRight: Uses the budget as an input to the decision, not the final arbiter.
rows.over: Manages to the budget rather than to the right thing for the customer or the employee.

rows.situation: When someone has to travel for the work
rows.under: Books business or first class as a habit.
rows.justRight: Travels coach with as few connections as will keep the person ready to do the job on arrival.
rows.over: Books the cheapest routing with extra connections to save a little money and burns the person's next two days.

rows.situation: When the spend is for the people who build
rows.under: Buys luxury that does not make anyone faster or more inventive.
rows.justRight: Spends on the tools, time, and environment that make builders faster, then is tight everywhere else.
rows.over: Cheaps out on the tools builders use every day, then wonders why the work is slow.

examples.title: Do not chew the two-by-fours
examples.body: You asked someone to build a house, then told them to chew through the lumber to save money. That is what cheap developer machines, broken build systems, and missing test environments look like. Frugality spends on the things that keep builders building, and invents everywhere else.

examples.title: Scale without matching the budget to traffic
examples.body: Traffic is on a path to grow well over 100 percent. The lazy answer is a matching budget. The frugal answer is a constraint (budget growth capped well below traffic growth) that forces a different architecture, a simpler deploy path, or a cheaper unit of compute. The constraint is the invention brief.

examples.title: Take the loss that buys the later payout
examples.body: A change will cost five million dollars this year and is likely worth $50 million later. The frugal leader can explain the unit economics and take the hit. The cheap leader kills it to protect this quarter. The wasteful leader cannot show the math at all.

looksLike.individual: An individual who is frugal knows what their work costs, and they treat time and other people's time as real money. They reuse before they buy. They can tell you the last time a constraint forced a better design. They do not wear thrift as a costume, and they do not hide waste behind "the customer needed it."
looksLike.manager: A manager who is frugal sets constraints that force invention, funds the tools and people that raise output, and refuses both the leftover-budget spend and the cut that breaks the customer. They pay for merit. They can explain a short-term loss that buys a long-term return. They do not keep score by headcount.

deepen: What constraint forced you to invent, and what did you build that you would not have built with a larger budget?
Where are you being cheap in a way that slows builders or hurts the customer?
If traffic or demand doubled, what would you refuse to scale linearly, and what would you have to reinvent?
Is this spend durable, or does it only make this quarter look better?
Are you spending leftover budget so nobody cuts you next year?
What is the unit cost of the thing you just asked to buy, and what happens to that unit cost if you change the design?
When did you last take a near-term loss on purpose because the longer-term payout was clear?
Which fixed expenses grew last year, and which of them bought no invention, no speed, and no customer value?
If you could not add headcount, how would you still get the outcome?

related.note: The constraint is the brief. Frugality without invention is just underfunding.
Owners spend as if the money is theirs and the long-term bill is theirs too.
Do not save money by shipping a worse product. That is cheap, not frugal.
The point of the saved resource is more result per unit of input, not a smaller dream.
